title: Lateen sails in Saint-Tropez: boats, gestures and analysis the harbour
author: Caramagnols
excerpt: This maritime gathering is not only about the shape of the sails. You also need to watch crews, quays, manoeuvres and the relation between the boats and the old harbour.
content:
Lateen sails become richer when you do not reduce them to a postcard image. The harbour, the crews and the gestures of mooring or preparation tell as much as the sails themselves, because they place the boats back into a living use.

The boat does not exist without the quay

In the old harbour, hulls make sense through mooring lines, distances between pontoons and the way each boat finds its place. The quay is not a neutral edge. It belongs to the scene and recalls that these boats come from a precise harbour culture.

Crew gestures give the scale

Preparing a sail, holding a yard, taking back a rope or passing instructions on board brings the event back to a human scale. It makes the effort, precision and technical transmission of this kind of navigation much easier to inspect, even when the boat is still.

Assess the harbour as a working space

Visitors gain by looking at the gathering as an active harbour rather than as a frozen historic set. This more concrete interpretation gives the event its full value, because it connects the image of the boats with real practice and the maritime memory of Saint-Tropez.
